claim: Stopping self-consistency sampling once the vote is stable cuts samples by roughly 2x to 5x on math and commonsense tasks with accuracy change near zero (about 0.1-1 point). Caveat from the gap search: the 2x-5x factors are measured against 40 samples. Against 16 samples ESC saves 4% to 71% (ReASC), and when each round re-sends the prompt, ASC and ESC can cost as much as or more than fixed SC (DSC Table 4: ASC +74%, ESC +3% on Mistral-7B GSM8K).
agent_test: Run fixed-N vote vs ESC window rule (w=5) vs Adaptive-Consistency on our agent at equal mean tokens; report accuracy and tokens per item.

claim: The savings from vote-stability stopping are uneven: large on easy data (GSM8K -80%, Coin Flip -84%, Boolean Expressions 7.9x) and small on hard data (MATH -33.8% with GPT-4; MATH500 offline acceptance only 7.2% for Llama-3.2-3B).
agent_test: Bin our items by base pass rate; plot token saving per bin.

claim: Difficulty-aware or reliability-aware stop rules cut a further 20-25% cost vs ESC at comparable accuracy (DSC -21.9 to -24.8% vs ESC; ReASC beats ASC and ESC on small models). Each result is the new method's own paper.
agent_test: Compare ESC vs DSC-style pre-allocation vs ReASC on our task set at matched accuracy, using our own implementation.

claim: Confidence-weighted voting (CISC) reaches fixed-SC accuracy with 31-46% fewer samples at budget 10; P(True) is the best confidence signal and verbalised binary confidence the worst; within-question discrimination is only 52-62% (chance 50%).
agent_test: Elicit a P(True)-style self-grade per sample; test if weighted vote beats plain vote at 10 samples.

claim: Token-level internal confidence can stop weak traces mid-generation and save 43-85% of tokens with accuracy about unchanged on AIME-type tasks (GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 -84.7%, 97.9% vs 97.1%). The headline 99.9% is a different mode (offline voting), not the same run as the savings.
agent_test: Check whether our API exposes token log-probs; otherwise use agreement among early partial answers as proxy.

claim: Coverage keeps rising with samples (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250; MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct 82.9% at 100 to 98.44% at 10,000) while majority vote and reward models plateau far below coverage. The selector, not the sampler, is the bottleneck.
agent_test: Measure the gap between pass@k and our selection rule at k=8 and 32; this gap bounds what better stopping or selecting can buy.

claim: Allocating test-time compute by estimated question difficulty matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute on MATH (PaLM 2-S*), and a smaller model with test-time compute beats a 14x larger one on easy and medium questions but not on the hardest or at high inference load.
agent_test: Estimate difficulty from 3-4 cheap samples, assign thinking budget, compare with uniform budget at equal mean tokens.

claim: Within one question, correct chains are shorter than wrong ones for o1-like models, and wrong answers average above 6,000 tokens vs under 3,000 when right on MATH.
agent_test: On our traces compute accuracy by length quantile within item; if the slope is negative, test a length cap with restart.

claim: Overthinking on easy items is real: o1-like models use 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on 2+3, the first solution round is correct in over 92% of cases using under 60% of tokens, and early exit cuts chains 19-80% with accuracy flat or up.
schema_part: G/O stop after first complete solution
agent_test: Add an answer-found check after the first complete solution round; compare with letting the model continue.

claim: Self-revision is a weak use of extra tokens: 58-72% of revisions by R1-family models keep the original wrong answer, successful revision rate is under 10%, and parallel sampling gives better coverage than sequential revision.
agent_test: Count right-to-wrong and wrong-to-right flips when our agent revises; keep revision only if net flips are positive.

claim: Forcing more thinking (budget forcing with Wait) gives small gains that flatten out: s1-32B AIME24 50.0 to 56.7 (2 problems of 30), MATH500 92.6 to 93.0, GPQA 56.6 to 59.6. Majority vote over 2-64 samples of the base stays below. The gain needs the Wait string (2x with no string stays 50.0).
agent_test: Forced re-check at the stop point vs no forcing at equal tokens, on at least 100 paired items because AIME24 has only 30.

claim: Length can be trained to follow a budget: L1 (1.5B, RL) beats s1 by 20-25 points absolute at 512 and 1024 tokens with length error 5.6-6.3%. Budget forcing has perfect controllability (100%) but the worst short-budget accuracy.
agent_test: Compare a prompted limit of N tokens with a hard cutoff on our agent: mean overshoot and accuracy.

claim: Training a model to reason only when it pays (reward: gain in answer log-likelihood minus a length cost) cuts output tokens 23-45% vs STaR and few-shot CoT with accuracy equal or up, and widens the easy/hard length gap (easy -50.3% for RaM vs -34.4% for STaR).
schema_part: none (needs training); scaffold analogue is G budget
agent_test: Scaffold analogue: score each step by change in answer log-prob (if available) and drop low-gain steps.

claim: People pick strategies and effort as value-of-computation predicts: sorting strategy choice adaptive on 83.0% of trials (model 70.5%); when thinking costs more they engage less (37% to 19% of trials) with reward per decision unchanged.
agent_test: Not directly testable on an LLM; supports a net-benefit stop rule.

claim: The ideal rule from rational metareasoning (stop when no available computation has expected value above its cost) is intractable in general. Cheap myopic or blinkered approximations exist, and the optimal policy computes whenever the myopic one does (Theorem 7), so myopic rules stop too early where one step is worth zero but several together pay.
agent_test: Implement the myopic rule as: does the next planned check change the leading answer with probability above cost over stake? Compare with vote-stability.

claim: Learned stop decisions in agent dialogues generalize badly if naive: base and SFT models stop worse than a fixed-turn rule out of distribution, while counterfactual-pair training (CaRT) fixes it. Only the abstract-level and training-recipe numbers were extracted.
agent_test: Test a fixed-turn rule vs a model-chosen stop on a held-out task family.

claim: Stop rules based on stated confidence alone are unsafe: verbalised confidence discriminates weakly within a question. Agreement among samples is the better-supported signal, but agreement fails when samples share a systematic error, which none of the studies tested directly.
agent_test: Compare stop by stated confidence vs by agreement at equal tokens; check calibration per bin and on items where all samples agree on a wrong answer.

claim: Vote-stability stopping measures agreement with SC-40, not correctness. The only direct count of wrong answers among early-accepted items is for single-sample confidence gates (ReASC): 1.4% to 8.7% wrong on GSM8K and 2.7% to 13.9% on MATH500, partly by design of the gate. No paper counts unanimous-wrong stops for vote rules. A simulation shows the wrong share of 4-unanimous stops ranges from under 1% to over 50%, set by how concentrated the model's wrong answers are, and different models do share wrong answers (60% agreement when both are wrong on HELM).
agent_test: On a labelled held-out set, log every item stopped at 4 unanimous votes and count how many are wrong, split by task and difficulty. Add a second-signal check (checker or different-prompt sample) and count how many it catches.

claim: Savings quoted against 40 or 512 samples shrink against a realistic small baseline and when input tokens are counted. Against 16 samples ESC saves 44.6% / 15.4% / 4.4% (GSM8K / MATH500 / Omni-Math) for Llama-3.2-3B and 71.4% / 56.6% (GSM8K / MATH500) for Gemma-3-27B. With the prompt re-sent per round, ASC costs 74% more and ESC 3% more than SC-40 on Mistral-7B GSM8K. Against a fixed best-of-4, adaptive resampling with a self-evaluation head gets more of the gain at 1.2 samples.
agent_test: Measure total tokens, input plus output, per item against fixed k=4, 8 and 16 baselines, not only 40.

claim: Coarse difficulty is cheap to estimate. A learned probe gets 72-84% median-split accuracy (Damani) and a simulated 4-sample pass-rate estimate gets 79-87%, but fine five-way bins need about 16 samples for 60-75% exact matches. Routing on a probe's errors can lose to a fixed budget at high compute (code, B>=8). Routing keeps most of the saving at coarse bins, but the 4x of Snell was not re-measured with a deployable estimator.
agent_test: Route on a 2-4 sample pass-rate class (easy, medium, hard) and compare tokens and accuracy with fixed best-of-4 and with oracle-binned allocation.

claim: Reflection or a forced re-check after the first answer mostly confirms it. In 8 reasoning models on 5 maths sets over 90% of reflections are confirmatory, wrong-to-right is under about 2%, first-candidate accuracy is within 1.4-3.5 points of final, and reflections take 16.8-47.8% of tokens. Without an outside label, prompted self-correction lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1); with an oracle stop it raises it (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5). The paired right-to-wrong rate for a forced Wait is still unreported.
agent_test: On the same items, run one pass vs one pass plus forced re-check; report flips split by first-answer correctness.

claim: For agent loops, a prompt-only signal exists: a visible remaining-budget counter lets ReAct agents use and save budget better than a hidden cap (BrowseComp 12.8 at budget 10 vs 10.3 for plain ReAct at 10 and 12.6 at 100; 31.3% lower cost; SWE-bench Verified 36.8 to 55.4 at budget 50). Stopping at the agent's own first verified answer lost 6-8 points against continuing. Trained stoppers (probes, CaRT, self-calibration) remain the other working route.
agent_test: Compare hidden turn cap, visible counter and model-chosen stop on one task family, with tokens and success.

claim: Where a real checker exists, stop-on-pass is far better than stop-on-agreement in principle (MATH Llama-3-8B: coverage 98.44% at 10,000 samples vs 41.41% for majority or reward-model selection). In practice checkers leak: 11.3% flaky SWE-bench Lite suites, 35 of 122 CodeContests problems with reference solutions failing their own tests, and a model's self-verification as a stop gave up 6-8 points in BATS. Stop-on-pass is only as good as the checker's false-pass rate.
agent_test: Measure the checker's false-pass rate on known-wrong outputs before using pass as a stop.

claim: Stop points should be set per model, not globally. Under agreement rules the stop point moves by itself (4.4x saving for GPT-3.5 vs 1.9x for Vicuna-13B). Under confidence gates it does not: ReASC acceptance rises with model size (GSM8K 49% to 61%, MATH500 7% to 37%) and the gate is calibrated to a target accuracy on held-out items.
agent_test: Calibrate the gate on 50-100 labelled items per model; compare with one global threshold.

claim: One router can choose across both models and reasoning modes. Route-to-Reason on Qwen3-4B gets 83.8% at 1,321 tokens vs 82.4% at 3,113 for always-think (-57.6% tokens) and 73.4% at 592 for never-think; over 7 models x 4 strategies it beats the best single model by 2.5 points with over 60% fewer tokens. Damani routes between decoders with 25-75% fewer expensive calls. Both are the authors' own comparisons and maths-heavy.
agent_test: Route per item between no-think, short think and long think using a cheap difficulty class; compare with the best fixed mode.

claim: No test was found of a myopic value-of-computation stop rule with a cost term against window-based stopping at equal tokens on an LLM. The nearest result: Bayesian posterior stability criteria (Beta, Dirichlet, CRP) beat raw vote-share and entropy rules at equal cost in Adaptive-Consistency (about 3% accuracy at 10 samples on GSM-8K).
agent_test: Implement: stop when P(next sample changes the leader) * stake < cost; compare with ESC window 4 at equal total tokens.

claim: Independent replication of DeepConf, DSC and ReASC is thin. Only one component was reused: the ReASC appendix reuses the bottom-10% group confidence of DeepConf and finds AUROC 0.860 against 0.801 for response-level confidence (Gemma-3-4B, MATH). No outside re-run of the DeepConf online stop or of DSC, and no run of any of the three outside maths, was found, though citation lookups were rate-limited.
agent_test: Re-run each stopper on a task family outside maths.
